<reason>PRO won by narrowing the clash to a decisive question: CON's "better alternative" (statutory inspection powers, published criteria, fines for refusal, written assessments to deployers) is itself a required evaluation with penalties, so the only live dispute is whether results should be standardized and public. CON defended that distinction competently (published adequacy criteria are not a common test battery; deployment risks differ from sandbox scores) and landed one real hit—PRO's honest A2 concession that publication adds no remedy for an empowered regulator, plus the point that aggregate refusal rates can't be reliably audited via API. But PRO answered its pressure questions directly and concretely (tiered disclosure design, multiplied actors, fraud liability for mandated filings, insurance against a captured single office), turned CON's own "customers may value capability over safety" worry into an argument for showing the tradeoff, and pressed CON's checklist and bespoke-comparability weaknesses. CON never squarely answered why one confidential office (or several) beats public verifiability, and its closing largely restated earlier points. PRO's two clipped turns are a minor execution cost, but PRO made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's R1/closing move that CON's alternative "is a mandate, with penalties, with publication" minus standardization and publication—reinforced by the pressure question on legal authority and CON's A1 answer that effectively confirmed statutory powers, published criteria, and fines—collapsed CON's case into a narrow disagreement about disclosure that PRO then weighed more convincingly.</best_rebuttal>
